title: Elara and the Echoing Woods
markdown:
Lumina Peaks Academy sat so high the towers looked like owls watching the world. Snow dusted the slate. The air had the fizz of a place where squirrels might argue geology and a griffin might mind the library doors.

Elara Meadowlight arrived with a worn satchel and a heart that would not sit still. She was not loud. Her talent was quieter: dragon wings softened their beat when she was near; a frost giant’s roar could be talked down to a sigh. She calmed the impossible, mostly by listening until the creature remembered it had a choice.

Her dorm mate, Jasper Stone, seemed unimpressed. His room was spotless, books ruler-straight, desk a landscape of diagrams and a spring that looked ready to start an incident. He eyed her unpacking as if he had seen it all and kept the receipt.

“So,” he drawled, not looking up. “You’re the one who makes shrieking mandrakes hum lullabies.”

Elara wrestled a knot on her trunk. “I try. They get distressed.”

“Try not to make them hum too loudly. Exams. And Professor Grumbles is still cross about the self-knitting scarves. Waste of wool, he says.”

It was the night before Open Day. Parents and hopefuls would flock up the mountain. The academy buzzed, from pixie polishers to the oldest dragon on the staff. Then, as the sun painted the peaks bruised purple, a sound began: a low thrum, like needles at the ear, then a storm of squeaks, roars, and squawks off the rock.

The Moon Moth colony, usually the school’s late-night lamps, flew frantic circles. Pale dust rained like anxious snow. Pixies who tended the flowerbeds pelted one another with dewdrop bombs, laughter gone sharp. Bartholomew, the ancient gargoyle on the highest turret, usually a grumbler about clouds, keened like a kettle with opinions.

Elara watched a herd of baby basilisks scatter, gazes luckily averted, and a moon-calf try a flagpole.

Jasper was already at the window, fingers tapping glass. “The resonance harmonizer. It’s amplifying distress. Someone will get singed, or itchy, or stared at by the wrong lizard.” He glanced at her. “You’re good with the ones that panic.”

Lumina Peaks bordered the Whispering Woods, paths like curious vines. The thrum was loudest there, an ache in the bone. Jasper took a reinforced walking stick and a look of grim usefulness. Elara followed, sorting cries from the din. A moth blundered against her cheek and left a smear of pale dust that itched exactly as advertised. Jasper did not offer a handkerchief. He did tap the stick once against a trunk, listening, as if the wood were a machine that had missed its service.

The forest erupted in sighs so large they shook leaves, then booming pronouncements. “The indignity. If only they knew of my magnificent fluff. A burden. A fluffy iridescent burden.”

Through a thicket they found the source on a mossy boulder: a creature like a particularly fluffy, grumpy cloud, round, iridescent grey, eyes that could melt frost. A Grumblepuff, famous for sighs and for being magnificently in the way. This one, Alaric, was mid-lament about exquisite grumbles and a world that would not understand his melancholies.

“He’s making it worse,” Jasper hissed. “Sonic pollution. We need the source, not a furry opera.”

“He seems upset,” Elara said, and her shyness stepped aside. Alaric puffed, fur bristling.

“Upset? I am bereft. The air groans. My fluff is heavy. And you two are disturbing me with scurrying. And frankly loud breathing.”

Elara smelled pine and damp earth and listened under the theatre. “It sounds like a lot to be unhappy about. It can be lonely when no one understands.”

Alaric blinked. For a professional dramatist, he looked surprised. “You understand? They tell me to cheer up. Or that my sighs bother the badgers. As if their grunts were music.”

As she spoke, the frantic thrum in the wood dimmed a notch. Alaric, mollified, explained with pauses and tragic declarations: he had been trying to warn the academy of a new hum from a hidden grove, a melancholy that ran through roots and, he suspected, all the way to the towers.

“This way,” he sniffed, pointing at a path that vanished into thorn. “The epicentre of unease. Do try not to tread on my tail. It’s despondent.”

He was a whirlwind of limbs and announcements, and also an astonishing guide. He stumbled over roots, called them an affront, then leapt them. He pointed out pitfalls that were not there, then found the one clear line through the tangle. He lamented a fallen leaf and darted ahead to scout mud.

They came into the grove the long way, because Alaric insisted a shorter path would offend a particular fern. The clearing was sun-dappled. A Lumina Sprite no bigger than a dewdrop hung there, wings a muted sorrowful blue, emitting a deep resonant hum that vibrated in the mountain. Elara understood at once. The academy’s new sound-enhancement system, built for Open Day lectures and songs, had caught the sprite’s melancholy and was broadcasting it, distorted, through every hall.

“The sprite,” she said. “Its sadness is being treated like a lecture.”

Jasper was already at the sonic conduits, fingers on cool humming metal. “Calibrated for speech and notes, not feeling. Feedback. You soothe it. I adjust the levels. Too quiet and the system cuts. Too loud and we get the banshee gargoyle again.”

Elara approached with empty hands and a steady breath. She did not give orders. She spoke of old loneliness, of a song that had been beautiful before it was made huge. Alaric sat uncharacteristically still on a log, fluff quiet, watching. The sprite’s hum softened at the edges into a sigh like wind in high trees.

Jasper’s hands flew over dials, a miniature tuning-fork switch among them. “Steady. Keep it flowing. There.”

The academy’s panic receded like a bad dream at dawn. Moon Moths settled to a peaceful pulse. Pixies remembered how to giggle about something other than bombs—possibly Alaric’s fur. Bartholomew produced a satisfied rumble that shook a loose slate and then, politely, did not do it again. Open Day, against the odds, would have a morning.

Later, on the quad, crowds thinning, faces still lit from phoenixes and other official wonders, Elara sat with Jasper and a much calmer Alaric, who was grooming with the concentration of a critic.

“I thought coming here would be about my talent. Doing it alone,” she said.

Jasper shrugged, and almost smiled. “Talents help. So does knowing which dial not to break. And,” a sideways look at Alaric, “knowing where the problem is hiding, even if you grumble the whole way.”

Alaric shimmered. “My grumbles are legendary. Perspective. Dramatic timing.”

Elara laughed, a sound kinder than any amplified sigh. Jasper leaned over to tap a wobbly turret bracket into honesty. Alaric hummed, contented, almost on key. The woods, behind the walls, kept their echoes. The school, for tonight, kept its moth-light.
characters: Elara Meadowlight (new pupil who can calm impossible creatures), Jasper Stone (a dorm mate who pretends not to care)
audience: children aged 11-12, fantastic mystery adventure for older children
